meta: How to use LordOS Imager · LordOS
Write LordOS to an SD card or a USB stick and set up the Raspberry Pi 5's first boot, screen by screen: device, system image, storage, customisation, writing and the first boot.
title: How to use LordOS Imager
lead: Write LordOS to an SD card or a USB stick from your computer and set up the Raspberry Pi 5's first boot. Screen by screen, in about ten minutes.
version: Version {v} · free and open source · collects nothing
alsoIn: Already on LordOS? It’s in App Launcher → System.
hello: Hi, I'm Lumo! I'll walk you through every screen.
need: With LordOS Imager installed, and an internet connection for the download.
An SD card or USB stick
16 GB or more is best (8 GB at the very least). Everything on it will be erased.
4 GB of memory at least, 8 GB or 16 GB for a smoother desktop. A fan and the 27 W power supply are recommended.
Most of it is the download and the write, which run by themselves.
videoLead: A short tour of every step, narrated in English, with subtitles in English, Spanish and Portuguese.
videoSoonText: Meanwhile, every step is below with its screenshot.
videoFallback: Your browser can't play this video. Download it:

steps.title: Choose your device
steps.text: Pick **Raspberry Pi 5** to prepare an SD card for the board, or **PC (USB stick)** to write the live system for a computer. Under the Pi, a bar shows how much memory it needs.
points: 4 GB is the minimum, 8 GB is comfortable and 16 GB gives the best performance.
Only boards LordOS really supports can be chosen.
shots: Step 1: the device, with the memory advice for the Raspberry Pi 5
tip: If your board isn't supported yet, I say so instead of letting you write a card that won't start.

steps.title: Choose the system image
steps.text: The latest LordOS release is already selected and marked **Signed by LordOS**. The download is kept, so the next card is quicker.
points: Older releases are one click away.
You can also use an image file of your own (`.img`, `.img.xz` or `.iso`). It's written and checked, but nobody vouches for where it came from.
shots: Step 2: the latest signed LordOS release
tip: Official images are checked against the LordOS release key before anything is erased.

steps.title: Choose the card or USB stick
steps.text: Insert the SD card (with a card reader if your computer needs one) or plug in the USB stick. It shows up by itself, with its name and size. Select it and read the red warning: everything on it will be erased.
points: Only removable drives are listed. Your computer's own disks never appear here.
A card that's too small or write-protected is shown greyed out, with the reason.
shots: Step 3: the SD card, selected, with the erase warning
tip: Copy anything you want to keep from the card first.

steps.title: Customise the first boot
steps.text: Leave **Prepare the first boot** on and the board starts ready: its name, your account, Wi-Fi, remote access, look and cooling. Seven tabs, and everything can be changed later in Settings. (For a PC stick there's nothing to customise: this step is skipped.)
subs: The **computer name** is how you'll find the board on your network: here `lordos-pi`, so `lordos-pi.local`. Then the language, time zone, keyboard layout and Wi-Fi country.
Your administrator account: full name, user name and a password typed twice. Only a one-way hash of the password goes on the card. Automatic login is optional.
The network name exactly as it appears (capitals count) and its password. The card keeps the network's derived key, never the password you typed. Hidden and open networks work too.
Remote login (SSH): off, keys only (recommended) or password and keys. You can also turn on LordOS remote desktop; it stays on your local network.
Lord Flow or Lord Classic, light or dark, an accent color and a wallpaper.
Tell LordOS what keeps the board cool and it picks the fan curve to match. Not sure? See [Which cooling do I have?](#cooling).
Only with a fan: 2.6 GHz instead of 2.4 GHz, with no extra voltage. The warning explains how to undo it.
Bluetooth, automatic update checks, and a promise: LordOS collects nothing.
Save these settings to reuse them for the next card. Passwords and Wi-Fi keys are never saved: you type them again.
tip: Your password and your Wi-Fi password never reach the card as they are: only a hash and a derived key.

steps.title: Check and write
steps.text: A summary of everything you chose, then **Erase and write** asks one last time. From there the imager does it all by itself:
points: checks the release signature, then downloads the image (an interrupted download resumes);
checks the image, writes it, then reads the whole card back and compares;
saves the first-boot settings and ejects the card.
shots: Downloading, with speed and time left
Reading the card back and comparing
tip: Cancel is safe: the card is cleared so it never looks half-written. The download is kept for next time.

steps.title: Done!
steps.text: Lumo celebrates and lists what comes next, with the exact name of your board on the network and the commands for remote login and remote desktop. A sound and a notification tell you it's finished.
shots: Done: written, verified and ejected, with the next steps

steps.title: The first boot on the Raspberry Pi 5
steps.text: Put the card in the board, connect the monitor, keyboard and mouse, then the power supply. The LordOS crown and a progress bar appear while the system grows to fill the card and applies your settings. After about a minute the login screen shows your account.
points: From another computer at home it's `lordos-pi.local`.
Remote desktop, if you turned it on: `https://lordos-pi.local:5673`.
boot: The boot screen while the first boot runs
The login screen (shown with example accounts)
tip: The settings file is applied once, then overwritten and deleted from the card.

coolLead: Pick what is physically on your board. It sets the fan curve and the clock speed, and you can change it later in Settings.
cool: A closed case with its own built-in fan, plugged into the board's fan connector. Many aluminium cases are like this.
Have a case with a fan? Choose **Case with a fan**.
A small heatsink with a fan on top that clips straight onto the board.
A metal case or a heatsink that cools without any fan.
A bare board. It works, but under load it slows itself down within minutes.
Choose **Nothing**: a gentler clock avoids that.
prof: With a fan (case or active cooler)
Balanced: the fan starts at 55 °C. Performance: from 45 °C, and the processor stays at full speed. Quiet: from 60 °C.
There's no fan to drive. Conservative caps the clock at 2.0 GHz.
2.0 GHz, so a bare board doesn't reach 85 °C and throttle.
ocText: 2.6 GHz instead of 2.4 GHz, with no extra voltage. Not every board is stable: if yours doesn't start, open the card's boot partition on another computer and delete the `lordos-firstrun` block in `config.txt`.
optText: **App options**, at the bottom of the sidebar: a sound and ejecting when finished, checking for app updates, language and appearance, and the download folder, with how much it uses and a button to clear it.
secLead: What LordOS Imager does to protect your card, your board and you.
sec: Before anything is erased, the release's list of files is checked against the LordOS release key, and the image's SHA-256 against that list. While writing, the image is hashed again.
After writing, the whole card is read back and compared with what was written.
It becomes a one-way hash before it's written. Wi-Fi is stored as the network's derived key.
The board checks the settings file strictly, applies it once, then overwrites and deletes it. An invalid file applies nothing.
Your computer's own disks are never listed, and your computer asks for an administrator's approval before the drive is opened.
No account, no usage data, no crash reports. The imager only talks to the LordOS releases page to list and download images.
faq: Only removable drives appear: SD cards and USB drives. Use a card reader if your computer has no slot, and wait a few seconds: the list updates by itself. A card whose lock switch is on, or one under 8 GB, is shown greyed out with the reason. Your computer's own disks are never shown, on purpose.
It says the signature didn't verify

Then nothing was written and nothing was erased. The downloaded files don't match what LordOS signed, usually because a download broke. Open **App options → Downloads → Clear** and try again. If it keeps happening, tell us (see the security page).
The board doesn't join my Wi-Fi

Check the network name (capitals count), the password and the Wi-Fi country in **General**. A network that only accepts WPA3 needs its password on the board itself: connect a network cable once and add it in **Settings → Network**.

Give the first boot a minute or two, and make sure your computer is on the same network (guest networks often keep devices apart). The login screen shows the board's address in its corner; you can use that address instead of the name.
How do I log in with SSH?

If you turned it on: `ssh demo@lordos-pi.local` (with your user name and computer name). Keys only is the safest choice. You can turn it on or off later in **Settings → Sharing**. The root account never logs in.
The board doesn't start after the overclock
Put the card in your computer, open its boot partition and delete the block between `# >>> lordos-firstrun` and `# <<< lordos-firstrun` in `config.txt`. The board starts at its normal speed again.
The board starts in setup mode and logs in by itself. Create your account in **Settings → Users**; on the next start the setup account is removed. Don't turn on remote desktop until then.
Can I write a USB stick for a PC?
Yes: choose **PC (USB stick)** in step 1. It writes the LordOS live system; boot the PC from the stick to try it, then install it from there.
endText: Free and open source. Every official image is checked against the release signature before anything is erased.
endOther: Prefer another way to write the card? See the download section.

home.title: How to write LordOS to a USB stick or SD card
home.lead: For the PC (ISO) and for the Raspberry Pi 5 image.
steps: Choose your device and the latest signed LordOS.
Pick the card or USB stick and, for the Pi, set up the first boot.
Write: it checks the signature, writes and reads the card back.
home.optTitle: Prefer your usual tool? That's fine.
home.optText: Download the ISO or the Raspberry Pi image from the release, check it against SHA256SUMS and write it with any image writer app, or with `dd`. `/dev/sdX` is the whole card or stick, not a partition.
home.optVerify: How to check the signature of SHA256SUMS
home.optPiSetup: Without LordOS Imager the Pi starts in setup mode. To prepare it, put `lordos-user.txt` and the switch files (`ssh`, `remote-desktop`) on the card's boot partition before the first boot.
